# The2026 veering-finiteness preprint and its precise consequences for parts(d) and(e)

**Problem:** TOP-2819

**Claim type:** Literature report

**Exact scope:** Reports Barthelmé–Tsang–Zung arXiv:2607.10398v2: finiteness of veering triangulations on compact orientable torus-boundary3-manifolds up to isotopy and finiteness of pseudo-Anosov flows without perfect fits up to isotopy, addressing parts(e) and(d). Other transitive-flow finiteness clauses are not asserted.

Parts(d) and(e) of the literal question have a direct recent primary source: Barthelmé–Tsang–Zung, arXiv:2607.10398v2, dated12August2026, titled *Finiteness of veering triangulations*. Theorem5.4 states that a compact orientable three-manifold with torus boundary has finitely many veering triangulations up to isotopy. Theorem5.9 states finiteness, up to isotopy equivalence, of pseudo-Anosov flows without perfect fits on a fixed closed three-manifold. These are reported as preprint theorems, not as new results of this contribution or as verified journal publications.

Both conclusions are strong enough for the specified equivalence conventions. Isotopy equivalence uses a homeomorphism isotopic to the identity, which in an oriented manifold preserves its orientation. Finiteness for that finer relation implies finiteness up to the problem's orbit equivalence. Likewise finiteness of isotopy classes of embedded veering triangulations implies finiteness of their underlying combinatorial classes. Restricting a finite collection to transitive flows preserves finiteness.

It is useful to isolate the actual mechanism, because “tight contact structures are finite” alone would not prove either statement. The main theorem fixes a closed oriented \(M\) and a fixed link \(L\). It considers flows possessing a positive Birkhoff section relative to \(L\), with a further strictness condition: every almost-transverse surface must meet \(L\). Drilling \(L\) allows the authors to construct a hypertight, Giroux-torsion-free contact structure with prescribed boundary germ, whose Reeb dynamics retain the pertinent free-homotopy spectrum of the original flow. Contact-finiteness and invariance of the cylindrical contact-homology data then reduce possible spectra to finitely many possibilities. A spectrum-classification theorem makes the possible flow isotopy classes finite, with at most a \(2^s\) ambiguity from scalloped Seifert pieces. These are the deep imported steps of their Theorem5.1.

For veering triangulations, it is not enough to assign each triangulation some unrelated Dehn filling. A common filling must work for an infinite hypothetical collection. The source's Lemma5.3 supplies the needed elementary step: from any sequence of nonzero torus multicurves, choose a slope intersecting an infinite subsequence at least three times. To check the idea, if every primitive slope had intersection at most two eventually, apply this to finitely many slopes \(3\lambda\pm\mu\) and \(\lambda\pm3\mu\). The resulting inequalities force both coordinates of each sufficiently late nonzero curve to vanish, a contradiction. Repeatedly taking subsequences handles the finitely many boundary tori.

Use those common slopes to fill the torus boundaries. The veering-to-flow correspondence gives pseudo-Anosov flows on one fixed filled manifold, with the filling cores as their singular orbits because the intersections are at least three. The source's Birkhoff-section theorem gives strict positivity relative to that fixed link. Its main fixed-link finiteness theorem now contradicts infinitely many distinct veering triangulations. The inverse correspondence is needed here; arbitrary association of triangulations to flows would not preserve distinctness. This is the structure of Theorem5.4.

For flows without perfect fits, the fixed-link hypothesis must again be justified. Theorem5.6 supplies finitely many possible isotopy classes of singular links and degeneracy data on a fixed atoroidal manifold. In that setting the source shows that positivity away from singularities is strict: an almost-transverse surface avoiding them would force a transverse torus, contrary to atoroidality. Passing to one of finitely many singular-link classes gives the fixed-link theorem. The no-perfect-fits situation supplies the required positive Birkhoff-section property; the special suspension case is handled separately. The authors combine these statements in Theorem5.9.

This account does not remove the fixed-link, strict-positivity or atoroidality hypotheses from the intermediate theorems. It also does not turn announced broader results mentioned in the preprint's discussion into checked proofs. In particular it does not assert finiteness of all transitive Anosov flows, all transitive pseudo-Anosov flows or all quasigeodesic pseudo-Anosov flows on every closed manifold, the distinct clauses(a)–(c) in the official prompt.

The report records substantive progress on two exact clauses and explains the quantifier-preserving passage from the fixed-link contact argument to those clauses. The primary theorem statements and those proof sections were read; the deep analytic and external classification machinery was not independently formalized or rerun. The paper is explicitly identified as the checked v2 preprint.
